exhibits.title: A message in metal
exhibits.summary: Before a screen could copy a sentence, someone arranged it one letter at a time.
exhibits.story: In movable-type printing, individual pieces carry raised characters. A printer arranges them into a page, applies ink, and presses paper against them. The same pieces can then be rearranged for a different page.
exhibits.look: Imagine pressing the letters onto paper. Which way would the printed letters face?
exhibits.connection: Copying a message changes who can hear it. Compare a printed page with a post shared online: who controls the original, and who can reproduce it?
exhibits.question: Why are the printing faces reversed?
choices: So the impression reads the right way around
To keep readers from copying them
exhibits.explanation: The impression is a mirror image of the type, so reversed type produces readable text.
exhibits.prompt: Find another object that shares information. What does it do better, and what does it lose?
exhibits.mysteryClue: My characters face backward, but my message comes out readable. What am I?

exhibits.title: The world in your pocket
exhibits.summary: A tiny needle can change an entire journey. But it cannot tell you everything.
exhibits.story: A magnetic compass uses a magnetized needle that aligns with the local magnetic field. Used with a map and an understanding of magnetic declination, it helps a traveler determine direction.
exhibits.look: Which part can move while the markings stay still? What could that help you work out?
exhibits.connection: A phone can show a route. A compass offers a direction. Think about what each tool depends on to work.
exhibits.question: What does a magnetic compass directly help you determine?
exhibits.explanation: A compass indicates direction; it does not directly provide location or distance.
exhibits.prompt: Find an object that helps someone solve a problem without electricity.
exhibits.mysteryClue: I can point you in a direction, but I cannot tell you your exact location. What am I?
exhibits.photoPhrase: Taking this visit in a new direction.

exhibits.title: Work, woven together
exhibits.summary: An everyday tool can reveal the skill hidden inside an everyday object.
exhibits.story: A weaving shuttle carries weft thread across the warp threads on a loom. Repeating this action helps build woven cloth. Shuttles vary with the loom, the fiber, and the weaver’s technique.
exhibits.look: Look at its shape. How might it carry thread through a narrow opening?
exhibits.connection: Check the fabric of your clothing. Can you see threads crossing, or loops? Woven and knitted textiles are made differently.
exhibits.question: What does a weaving shuttle carry?
exhibits.explanation: The shuttle carries the weft across the warp threads.
exhibits.prompt: Find something that required repeated hand movements to make. What skill might its maker have practiced?
exhibits.mysteryClue: I carry thread across other threads, helping turn repeated movements into cloth. What am I?

exhibits.title: Replica Hand Axe
exhibits.period: Style used from about 1.7 million to 130,000 years ago
exhibits.material: To be verified for the actual collection
exhibits.summary: Long before our species appeared, early human ancestors in Africa shaped stones like this one by striking them with harder rocks. A hand axe could cut meat, chop wood, and dig for roots. This is a modern replica made the same way.
exhibits.story: Long before our species appeared, early human ancestors in Africa shaped stones like this one by striking them with harder rocks. A hand axe could cut meat, chop wood, and dig for roots. This is a modern replica made the same way.
exhibits.look: Pick one edge and one place you might grip. What makes you think each would work?
exhibits.connection: Hand axes are one of the longest-used tools in history. People made them in nearly the same shape for over a million years.
exhibits.question: What does this replica help us investigate?
choices: How early people made and used stone tools
exhibits.explanation: How early people made and used stone tools. Hand axes are one of the longest-used tools in history. People made them in nearly the same shape for over a million years.
exhibits.prompt: What is a tool you use every day? How long do you think people will keep using it?
exhibits.mysteryClue: Hand axes are one of the longest-used tools in history. People made them in nearly the same shape for over a million years.
exhibits.photoPhrase: A cutting-edge idea. For its time.

exhibits.title: Replica Oracle Bone
exhibits.material: To be verified for the actual collection
exhibits.summary: Rulers of China's Shang dynasty asked questions about the future by carving them into bones and turtle shells, then heating them until they cracked. The carvings are the oldest known Chinese writing.
exhibits.story: Rulers of China's Shang dynasty asked questions about the future by carving them into bones and turtle shells, then heating them until they cracked. The carvings are the oldest known Chinese writing.
exhibits.look: Look for marks made on purpose. How would you distinguish an inscription from a crack?
exhibits.connection: Some characters on oracle bones still look a lot like Chinese characters used today.
exhibits.question: What were oracle bones used for?
exhibits.explanation: Questions and divination. Some characters on oracle bones still look a lot like Chinese characters used today.
exhibits.prompt: If you could ask one question about the future, what would it be?
exhibits.mysteryClue: Some characters on oracle bones still look a lot like Chinese characters used today.

exhibits.title: Cave Painting Panel (Reproduction)
exhibits.material: To be verified for the actual collection
exhibits.summary: Ice Age artists painted horses, bulls, and deer deep inside caves using red and yellow ochre and black charcoal. This panel is a hand-painted reproduction of animals from the Lascaux cave.
exhibits.story: Ice Age artists painted horses, bulls, and deer deep inside caves using red and yellow ochre and black charcoal. This panel is a hand-painted reproduction of animals from the Lascaux cave.
exhibits.look: Which few lines let you recognize an animal? Trace them in the air.
exhibits.connection: The real Lascaux cave was discovered in 1940 by four teenagers following their dog.
exhibits.question: Which detail connects this reproduction to Ice Age art?
exhibits.explanation: Painted animals and mineral pigments. The real Lascaux cave was discovered in 1940 by four teenagers following their dog.
exhibits.prompt: Why do you think people painted animals in dark caves where few could see them?
exhibits.mysteryClue: The real Lascaux cave was discovered in 1940 by four teenagers following their dog.

exhibits.title: Cranberry Harvest Scoop
exhibits.material: To be verified for the actual collection
exhibits.summary: Workers in the Pine Barrens used wooden scoops with long teeth to comb cranberries off the vines. New Jersey has grown cranberries for more than 150 years and is still one of the top cranberry states.
exhibits.story: Workers in the Pine Barrens used wooden scoops with long teeth to comb cranberries off the vines. New Jersey has grown cranberries for more than 150 years and is still one of the top cranberry states.
exhibits.look: Look at the gaps between the teeth. What could slip through, and what would stay in the scoop?
exhibits.connection: Cranberries have pockets of air inside, so they float. Farmers flood the bogs and the berries rise to the top.
exhibits.question: Why would spaced teeth work better than a solid blade for picking cranberries?
choices: They seal the scoop so water stays inside.
They let thin vines pass between the teeth while the berries are caught.
They cut the roots so the whole plant comes out.
exhibits.explanation: The spaces let thin stems pass through while the wider berries catch against the teeth. Look again at the spacing on the scoop.
exhibits.prompt: What crops or foods come from near where you live?
exhibits.mysteryClue: Cranberries have pockets of air inside, so they float. Farmers flood the bogs and the berries rise to the top.
